exam: What are the three phases of normal wound healing and how does diabetes alter them? — Describe haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation; note delayed inflammation and reduced collagen synthesis in diabetes.

A patient with a 3‑cm laceration contaminated with soil presents 12 h after injury. What is your next step? — Irrigate, debride, give tetanus booster, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering soil organisms.

How do you differentiate a dirty wound from a clean‑contaminated wound on exam? — Dirty wounds have gross contamination, devitalised tissue, or delayed presentation; clean‑contaminated are operative incisions with controlled exposure.

A child with a deep puncture wound on the foot develops increasing pain and swelling despite oral antibiotics. What is the most likely complication and immediate management? — Suspect necrotising fasciitis; arrange urgent surgical debridement and IV broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
Explain why fluoroquinolones are avoided in paediatric wound infections. — Risk of tendon rupture and cartilage toxicity; safer alternatives exist.

What laboratory investigations would you order if you suspect malnutrition is impairing wound healing, and how would you act if they are unavailable? — Serum albumin and HbA1c; if unavailable, assess clinical nutrition and provide high‑protein diet.

Describe the Gustilo‑Anderson classification for open fractures and the corresponding antibiotic choice. — Grade I: simple wound, give cefazolin; Grade II: moderate soft‑tissue injury, cefazolin; Grade III: extensive soft‑tissue damage, add aminoglycoside.
When is tetanus immunoglobulin indicated for a wound? — When the wound is dirty, the patient’s immunisation status is unknown or >10 years since last dose, and the patient is not fully immunised.

ai.summary: Practical approach to assessing, classifying and treating wounds where diagnostics and supplies are limited. Emphasises bedside decision‑making, common tropical infections and when to seek urgent help.

b: Primary vs secondary intention healing
Clean, contaminated, dirty classifications (Gustilo‑Anderson for open fractures)
Key goals: prevent infection, promote granulation, restore function
sections.p: Wounds are breaches of skin or mucosa that may be traumatic, surgical or chronic. In low‑resource hospitals the clinician must rely on history, visual inspection and simple tools to guide care.

b: Host factors: diabetes, HIV, malnutrition, peripheral vascular disease
Microbial risk: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, anaerobes, tropical pathogens (e.g., Mycobacterium ulcerans, Burkholderia pseudomallei)
Healing phases: haemostasis → inflammation → proliferation → remodeling
sections.p: Understanding the wound environment, host factors and microbial threats drives management.

b: History: mechanism, time since injury, tetanus status, comorbidities
Examination: size, depth, edges, presence of foreign material, signs of infection (redness, warmth, pus, foul odor)
Classification: use the WHO/UNICEF wound grading for pressure ulcers; for traumatic wounds apply the Clean‑Contaminated‑Dirty scheme
sections.p: A systematic bedside assessment identifies severity, guides debridement and antibiotic choice, and predicts complications such as sepsis or chronic ulceration.

t.a: Gram stain / microscopy of wound swab
t.b: Identifies predominant organisms and guides empiric antibiotics; if unavailable, treat empirically based on likely flora
Assesses glycaemic control which impacts healing; if unavailable, use random glucose
Detects malnutrition; low levels predict delayed healing; if unavailable, use clinical nutrition assessment

t.a: X‑ray of limb (if deep or penetrating injury)
t.b: Detects retained foreign bodies or bone involvement; if unavailable, rely on careful palpation and plain clinical suspicion

b: Initial irrigation with clean water or saline; avoid high‑pressure jets that damage tissue
Debridement: remove devitalised tissue surgically or with enzymatic agents if theatre unavailable
Antibiotics: give broad‑spectrum covering Gram‑positive, Gram‑negative and anaerobes (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) when infection is likely; avoid fluoroquinolones in children due to tendon risk
Tetanus prophylaxis: give tetanus toxoid if >5 years since last dose, or tetanus immunoglobulin if wound is dirty and immunisation unknown
Dressings: use sterile gauze, honey dressings, or locally available boiled cotton; change daily or when soiled
Nutrition: encourage high‑protein diet, oral supplements if albumin low
Monitoring: check for increasing pain, expanding erythema, fever – signs of spreading infection
sections.p: Treat the cause first, then support tissue repair.

b: Distinguish clean vs dirty wounds – dirty wounds need immediate antibiotics
Know the Gustilo‑Anderson grades for open fractures and corresponding antibiotic regimens
Identify when a wound is a surgical emergency (e.g., necrotising fasciitis) – requires urgent debridement
sections.p: Exam questions often test classification, choice of empiric antibiotics and recognition of complications.

b: Using topical antibiotics alone for a dirty wound – does not replace systemic therapy
Delaying debridement because of lack of theatre – can be performed bedside with sterile instruments
Ignoring host factors such as uncontrolled diabetes, which markedly impairs healing
sections.p: Pitfalls arise from over‑reliance on unavailable tests or inappropriate dressings.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading erythema or edema (possible necrotising fasciitis)
High fever >38.5 °C with tachycardia and hypotension
Severe pain out of proportion to wound appearance
